basics: Think of the kidneys as a regulated filter and the other three organs as pipes and a tank. The kidneys' real job is homeostasis of the blood, not just waste removal: they decide how much water and which ions (Na+, K+, Ca2+, Cl−, phosphate) stay in the body, which sets blood volume and hence blood pressure; they dump or keep H+ and bicarbonate, which sets blood pH; they can make new glucose from amino acids when fasting; and they are endocrine organs, releasing renin (an enzyme that starts the angiotensin pressure-raising cascade), erythropoietin (drives red-cell production) and calcitriol (active vitamin D, for calcium). Waste excretion covers urea, ammonia, creatinine, uric acid and drugs. The slide lists outcomes but not the mechanisms; the rest of the lecture explains how filtering, reabsorbing and secreting achieve them.

basics: Each kidney is a bean about 11 cm long with its concave edge facing the spine. In the middle of that concave edge is a slot, the hilum, which is the only doorway into the organ: the renal artery enters, the renal vein and the ureter leave, and nerves and lymphatic vessels pass through alongside them. Inside, the hilum opens into a cavity (the renal sinus) that houses the renal pelvis and the branching vessels. The vascular arrangement is simple: the aorta gives a renal artery to each kidney, and each kidney returns blood by a renal vein straight into the inferior vena cava. Because the aorta lies left of the midline and the vena cava right of it, the left renal vein is long and the right renal artery is long, as slide 3's figure shows. The slide does not mention that the kidney receives about a fifth of cardiac output despite being under 0.5% of body mass.

basics: This is a horizontal slice through the abdomen at the second lumbar vertebra, viewed from below (so the patient's right is on the viewer's left). basics: Cut the kidney lengthwise and two zones appear: a pale outer rind (cortex) and a darker inner region (medulla) made of 8–18 cone-shaped renal pyramids. Cortex tissue also dips down between the pyramids as renal columns. Cortex plus pyramids form the parenchyma — the working tissue — and inside it are about a million nephrons, the microscopic filtering-and-processing units. Each pyramid's tip (papilla) points inward and drips urine into a small cup (minor calyx); several minor calyces join into 2–3 major calyces, which merge into the renal pelvis, which narrows into the ureter. Once fluid reaches the calyces it is final urine: the lining changes to a leak-proof urothelium so nothing more can be reabsorbed. The renal sinus is the fat-filled cavity inside the hilum that holds the pelvis, calyces and vessels. The slide's 'renal lobe' label anticipates slide 10.

basics: The kidney cleans blood, so blood must reach every nephron: with only ~0.5% of body mass it takes 20–25% of the heart's resting output, about 1.2 L/min. The arterial tree branches in a fixed order you should be able to recite: renal artery → segmental arteries → interlobar arteries (running up the renal columns between pyramids) → arcuate arteries (arching over the base of each pyramid at the cortex–medulla border) → cortical radiate (interlobular) arteries (radiating out through the cortex) → afferent arterioles, one per nephron. Each afferent arteriole feeds a ball of capillaries (glomerulus) that drains into an efferent arteriole — unusual, because capillaries normally drain into a venule. The efferent arteriole then feeds a second capillary bed (peritubular capillaries, plus the long vasa recta into the medulla) before veins retrace the same names back to the renal vein. A renal lobe is one pyramid with the cortex over it and half a column each side.

basics: A nephron is a single filtering unit; you have about a million per kidney. It has two parts. The renal corpuscle is a capillary ball (glomerulus) pushed into a double-walled cup (glomerular or Bowman's capsule); plasma is squeezed out of the capillaries into the cup. The renal tubule then carries that filtrate along a set path: proximal convoluted tubule (coiled, in the cortex) → nephron loop (loop of Henle: a straight descending limb into the medulla, hairpin, ascending limb back) → distal convoluted tubule (coiled, in the cortex) → collecting duct (shared by many nephrons; not strictly part of the nephron) → papillary duct → minor calyx. The slide's percentages classify nephrons by where the corpuscle sits: cortical nephrons (80–85%) have corpuscles in the outer cortex and short loops that barely enter the medulla; juxtamedullary nephrons (15–20%) have corpuscles next to the medulla and long loops reaching deep into it, which is what allows very concentrated urine (slide 33).

basics: Zoom into one renal corpuscle. The glomerulus is a tuft of capillaries hanging between an afferent arteriole (in) and an efferent arteriole (out). Around it is the glomerular (Bowman's) capsule, which has two layers because it is like a balloon that a fist has been pushed into: the visceral layer (cells called podocytes) hugs the capillaries, the parietal layer forms the outer wall, and the gap between them, the capsular space, is where filtrate collects before draining into the PCT. Mesangial cells sit between the capillary loops and can contract to change the filtering area. The juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) is where the same nephron's ascending limb loops back to touch its own afferent arteriole: a patch of tall tubule cells (macula densa) senses salt in the tubular fluid, and modified smooth-muscle cells in the arteriole wall (juxtaglomerular cells) release renin. This lets each nephron monitor its own filtration rate and adjust arteriole diameter and blood pressure (slides 21–23).

basics: The whole tubule is one cell thick, but the cell type changes segment by segment, and form follows function. PCT: cuboidal cells with a dense brush border of microvilli and many mitochondria — huge surface area and lots of ATP for the bulk reabsorption that happens here (about two-thirds of everything). Descending limb and thin ascending limb: flat squamous cells — a thin, passive wall suited to water or solute movement down gradients. Thick ascending limb: cuboidal-to-low-columnar cells rich in pumps — active salt transport, no water. Most of the DCT: plain cuboidal cells for fine-tuning. Late DCT and collecting duct: cuboidal epithelium of two kinds — principal cells (respond to ADH and aldosterone; handle Na+, K+ and water) and intercalated cells (secrete H+ or bicarbonate; acid–base control). The slide shows the table only; the functional meaning of each cell type is what slides 25–31 develop.

p.1053 right column: the introductory paragraph under '26.4 Overview of Renal Physiology' (starts 'To produce urine, nephrons and collecting ducts…'); continues on p.1054 below the figure as numbered items 1 Glomerular filtration, 2 Tubular reabsorption, 3 Tubular secretion (left column) and the two paragraphs in the right column (excretion = filtration + secretion − reabsorption; the recycling-centre analogy)

basics: Urine is made by three operations, and every later slide is one of them. (1) Glomerular filtration: pressure pushes water and small solutes out of the glomerular capillaries into the capsule — a crude sieve that lets through everything smaller than proteins, so the filtrate is essentially protein-free plasma. (2) Tubular reabsorption: as the filtrate travels along the tubule and collecting duct, the lining cells take back about 99% of the water and the useful solutes and hand them to the peritubular capillaries — 'reabsorption' because these substances were already in the blood. (3) Tubular secretion: the same cells move extra material (H+, K+, ammonium, creatinine, drugs) from the blood into the tubule. What leaves in the urine equals filtered plus secreted minus reabsorbed. Note the direction words on the figure: reabsorption goes tubule → blood, secretion goes blood → tubule.

Transfer of substances from blood or tubule cells into the tubular fluid.
What finally leaves the body in urine.
Absorption brings new material into the body (gut); reabsorption returns what was already in blood.
Any dissolved substance, e.g. ions, glucose, urea.

title: The filtration membrane

refs.capture: p.1055 Figure 26.8 part (a) 'Overview of filtration membrane' (lower half of the page, with the three numbered layer descriptions); continued on p.1056 as parts (b) 'Details of filtration membrane' and (c) SEM of a podocyte covering a glomerulus (upper left of the page) – the slide reproduces these

basics: Filtration is sieving: what passes depends on pore size and charge. Between blood and capsular space there are three layers, each finer than the last. (1) The capillary endothelium is riddled with round pores (fenestrations, ~0.07–0.1 µm) that stop blood cells but let all plasma solutes through. (2) The basement membrane, a gel of collagen and negatively charged glycoproteins made jointly by the endothelial cells and podocytes, blocks large proteins by size and repels most plasma proteins by charge. (3) The podocyte foot processes (pedicels) interdigitate, leaving filtration slits bridged by a slit membrane whose openings (~0.006–0.007 µm) exclude medium-sized proteins; albumin is just too big, so under 1% gets through. Water, ions, glucose, amino acids, urea and small peptides pass freely. The take-home number the slide leaves off: the whole membrane is only ~0.1 µm thick, and glomerular capillaries are about 50 times leakier than ordinary ones.

terms.d: The three-layer barrier (endothelium, basement membrane, podocyte slits) between glomerular blood and capsular space.

title: Pressures that govern glomerular filtration rate

refs.capture: p.1057 Figure 26.9 'The pressures that drive glomerular filtration' (upper half of the page, including the NFP calculation box on the right: 55 − 15 − 30 = 10 mmHg) – the slide reproduces this figure

basics: This is Starling's capillary balance applied to the glomerulus. Fluid crosses a membrane when the net pressure across it is positive. Pushing outward is the blood's hydrostatic pressure in the glomerular capillaries (GBHP ≈ 55 mmHg — unusually high because the exit arteriole is narrower than the entry arteriole, so blood backs up). Pushing back are two opposing pressures: the hydrostatic pressure of fluid already sitting in the capsule and tubule (CHP ≈ 15 mmHg), and the osmotic pull of plasma proteins that stayed behind in the blood (blood colloid osmotic pressure, BCOP ≈ 30 mmHg — water is drawn back toward the more concentrated protein solution). Net filtration pressure = 55 − 15 − 30 = 10 mmHg outward. Only 10 mmHg, but over a vast, extremely leaky surface it filters ~180 L/day. If GBHP falls to 45 mmHg (severe blood loss), filtration stops; if a ureter is blocked, CHP rises and NFP falls.

terms.d: Pressure exerted by a fluid pushing on the walls containing it.

basics: GFR is the volume of filtrate all two million corpuscles make per minute: ~125 mL/min in males, ~105 mL/min in females, i.e. 150–180 L/day — the entire plasma volume (~3 L) filtered about 60 times a day. Since urine output is only 1–2 L, more than 99% of the filtrate must be reabsorbed. The slide's first bullets restate slide 19: GFR is driven by glomerular capillary pressure, which is set by the relative diameters of the afferent (in) and efferent (out) arterioles, and opposed by capsular pressure and plasma protein osmotic pressure. Filtration is by size, so cells and proteins stay in the blood. GFR must be held nearly constant: too high and useful solutes rush past before they can be reclaimed; too low and wastes are not cleared. The next three slides cover the three regulators: renal autoregulation, sympathetic nerves, and hormones. Strictly, it is the capillary pressure between the two arterioles that matters.

basics: Autoregulation means the kidney holds its own blood flow and GFR steady across everyday swings in arterial pressure (roughly 80–180 mmHg) without help from nerves or hormones. The myogenic mechanism is a property of vascular smooth muscle itself: when arterial pressure rises, the afferent arteriole wall is stretched, and stretched smooth muscle responds by contracting, which narrows the lumen, cuts the flow into the glomerulus, and brings GFR back down. When pressure falls, the wall is stretched less, relaxes, the arteriole widens and GFR recovers — the 'vice versa' of the slide. This works within seconds. Read the slide's arrow chain as a negative-feedback loop: the rise in GFR is the disturbance and the constriction is the correction. The second autoregulatory mechanism, tubuloglomerular feedback, is slower and uses the JGA (next slide).

terms.d: Originating in muscle itself (myo- muscle, -genic producing), without nerve input.

basics: The second autoregulatory loop uses the nephron's own tubule as a flow meter. If GFR rises, filtrate rushes through the PCT and loop faster than the cells can reabsorb Na+, Cl− and water, so more salt arrives at the macula densa — the sensor patch in the ascending limb that sits against the afferent arteriole (slide 14). The macula densa cells respond by reducing the release of nitric oxide (NO) from the juxtaglomerular apparatus. NO is a vasodilator, so less NO means the afferent arteriole constricts, less blood enters the glomerulus, and GFR falls back. A drop in GFR triggers the reverse, more weakly. Because it depends on fluid travelling the length of the tubule, this loop is slower than the myogenic one. Note the naming: 'tubulo-glomerular' because the tubule signals the glomerulus; it is a local, nephron-by-nephron control.

basics: Beyond the kidney's local autoregulation, the body can override GFR for whole-body needs. Neural control: sympathetic nerves release norepinephrine onto α1 receptors on arteriolar smooth muscle. At rest their activity is low and autoregulation dominates; moderate activity constricts afferent and efferent arterioles equally and barely changes GFR; strong activity (exercise, haemorrhage) constricts the afferent arteriole preferentially, cutting renal blood flow and GFR — which conserves blood volume and diverts blood to muscle and brain. The same nerves stimulate renin release. Hormonal control: angiotensin II, produced when blood volume or pressure is low, is a powerful constrictor of both arterioles and lowers GFR (keeping fluid in the body). Atrial natriuretic peptide, released when the atria are stretched by excess blood volume, relaxes mesangial cells, enlarging the filtering surface and raising GFR so that more salt and water are excreted.

basics: The tubule wall is a single sheet of cells joined near their tops by tight junctions, like a six-pack of cans held by a plastic ring: the top of each can (apical membrane) faces the tubular fluid, the sides and bottom (basolateral membrane) face the interstitial fluid and the peritubular capillary. A reabsorbed molecule therefore has two possible paths. Paracellular: slip passively between the cells through the tight junction; in the PCT the junctions are leaky enough that up to half of some ions, with water following by osmosis, take this route. Transcellular: cross the apical membrane into the cell, traverse the cytoplasm, and exit across the basolateral membrane — which requires transport proteins and allows the cell to control what moves and in which direction. Either way the substance ends up in the interstitial fluid and diffuses into the capillary. The slide names the routes; the mechanism (Na+ pumps and gradients) is on the next slide.

basics: Glucose is freely filtered (about 160 g/day) yet none appears in normal urine, so the PCT must reclaim all of it, along with amino acids, lactate and water-soluble vitamins. The trick is secondary active transport driven by sodium. Basolateral Na+/K+ pumps keep the cell's Na+ low, so Na+ 'wants' to enter from the tubular fluid. An apical symporter (SGLT) only lets Na+ in if a glucose molecule rides along, so the sodium gradient drags glucose into the cell even against its own gradient; glucose then leaves the basolateral side by facilitated diffusion and enters the capillary. Other symporters do the same for phosphate, sulfate, amino acids and lactate; antiporters swap Na+ in for H+ out (next slide). Every transporter has a maximum rate (Tm): if blood glucose exceeds roughly 200 mg/dL, as in untreated diabetes, the symporters saturate and glucose spills into urine (glucosuria), pulling water with it osmotically.

basics: The second sodium-linked device in the PCT is the Na+–H+ antiporter: each Na+ that enters the cell down its gradient pushes one H+ out into the tubular fluid. So sodium is reabsorbed (it exits basolaterally via the Na+/K+ pump) and acid is secreted in the same step. Where does the H+ come from? The cell makes it. CO2 — diffusing in from blood or tubular fluid, or produced by the cell's own metabolism — combines with water under the enzyme carbonic anhydrase to give carbonic acid (H2CO3), which immediately splits into H+ and bicarbonate (HCO3−). The H+ feeds the antiporter; the HCO3− leaves across the basolateral membrane into the blood, replenishing the body's main buffer. That is the slide's two bullets. The slide title is 'sodium' but the important consequence is acid–base: this is how the kidney excretes acid and generates bicarbonate, and angiotensin II stimulates this antiporter to boost Na+ and water retention.

basics: Bicarbonate is filtered in large amounts (~275 g/day) and the body cannot afford to lose it, but the apical membrane has no bicarbonate transporter. The kidney solves this indirectly. The H+ secreted by the Na+–H+ antiporter (slide 26) meets filtered HCO3− in the lumen and forms carbonic acid, which breaks down (helped by carbonic anhydrase on the brush border) into CO2 and water. Inside, carbonic anhydrase re-forms carbonic acid, which splits again into H+ and HCO3−: the H+ is recycled out through the antiporter and the 'new' HCO3− exits basolaterally into the blood with Na+. Net result per cycle: one filtered bicarbonate is effectively moved from lumen to blood, one Na+ is reabsorbed, and no acid is lost. About 80% of filtered bicarbonate is reclaimed this way in the PCT; intercalated cells in the collecting duct finish the job (slide 30).

basics: Everything so far used pumps; this slide shows what happens for free. In the first half of the PCT the active reabsorption of Na+, glucose, bicarbonate and so on raises the solute concentration in the cell, then in the interstitium, then in the capillary. Water follows by osmosis — through the leaky junctions and through aquaporin-1 water channels that make PCT and descending-limb cells highly water-permeable. As water leaves, the solutes left behind in the tubular fluid (Cl−, K+, Ca2+, Mg2+, urea) become more concentrated than in the interstitium, so in the second half of the PCT they diffuse out down their gradients, para- and transcellularly. Chloride, the most abundant, leaves first and makes the interstitium electrically negative, which then pulls the positive ions after it. So about 65% of water and most ions leave the PCT with no extra energy, and the fluid stays isosmotic (~300 mOsm/L) with plasma throughout.

basics: By the time fluid leaves the PCT, 65% of its water and nearly all nutrients are gone, but because water and solute left together the fluid is still isosmotic with blood (~300 mOsm/L). The loop changes that: for the first time water and salt are handled separately. The descending limb is permeable to water but not salt, so water is drawn out into the increasingly salty medulla (~15% of filtered water). The thick ascending limb is the opposite: its apical Na+–K+–2Cl− symporters pull salt out (about 25% of filtered Na+ and K+, 35% of Cl−), K+ leaks back into the lumen making the interstitium negative and dragging more cations out paracellularly, but the wall is essentially watertight, so the fluid becomes progressively more dilute (down to 100–150 mOsm/L) while the medullary interstitium gets saltier. This separation is what lets the kidney later choose to excrete dilute or concentrated urine. Loop diuretics such as furosemide block these symporters.

basics: About 90% of water reabsorption is obligatory (it simply follows solute in the PCT and descending limb). The last ~10%, in the late DCT and collecting duct, is facultative — switched on or off to suit the body's water balance — and the switch is ADH. Without ADH, principal cells are almost watertight. ADH makes vesicles packed with aquaporin-2 water channels fuse into the apical membrane; water can then flow from the dilute tubular fluid into the cell and out through the always-permeable basolateral side into the blood. The control loop: if you lose water, plasma osmolarity rises (water concentration falls); osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect a change as small as 1% and drive ADH release from the posterior pituitary; more water is reabsorbed, osmolarity falls back, ADH release slows. In diabetes insipidus, absent ADH (or unresponsive kidneys) means the switch is never thrown, so up to 20 L of very dilute urine can be passed daily.

basics: Follow the numbers on Figure 26.18. Filtrate enters at 300 mOsm/L, the same as plasma, and is still 300 leaving the PCT. Down the descending limb water is pulled out into the salty medulla, so the fluid concentrates (up to ~900 at the tip of a long loop). basics: To make urine more concentrated than plasma the kidney needs a place saltier than plasma to draw water into: the medullary interstitium, whose osmolarity climbs from 300 at the cortex to 1200 mOsm/L at the papilla. Only the long loops of juxtamedullary nephrons build this gradient, by countercurrent multiplication. The thick ascending limb pumps NaCl out into the interstitium but keeps water; the neighbouring descending limb, carrying fluid the opposite way, loses water to that salty interstitium and so delivers ever-saltier fluid to the ascending limb, which pumps out still more salt — each pass 'multiplies' the difference, and urea recycled from the collecting duct adds to the deep-medullary solute. When ADH makes the collecting duct water-permeable, fluid passing through this gradient loses water by osmosis and exits at up to 1200 mOsm/L. The hairpin vasa recta (countercurrent exchange) pick up salt going down and return it coming up, feeding the medulla without washing out the gradient.

basics: Because urine is the end product of filtration, reabsorption and secretion, its composition is a window onto the kidney and the body. Normal urine is ~95% water with urea, creatinine, uric acid, urobilinogen and electrolytes, and essentially no protein, glucose or cells. Each abnormal finding points to a failed step. Albumin (albuminuria): the filtration membrane has become leaky — damage, high pressure, toxins. Glucose (glucosuria): filtered load exceeded the PCT transport maximum, almost always diabetes mellitus. Red cells (haematuria): bleeding somewhere from glomerulus to urethra — inflammation, stones, tumours. Ketone bodies (ketonuria): the body is burning fat for lack of usable carbohydrate — diabetes, starvation, anorexia. Urobilinogen: a haemoglobin breakdown product; excess suggests haemolysis or liver/bile-duct disease. Microbes: urinary tract infection, most often E. coli. The slide shows only the dipstick side; the book also covers blood urea nitrogen, plasma creatinine, and clearance (inulin or creatinine clearance ≈ GFR).

basics: Once fluid reaches the calyces it is urine and is simply moved and stored. Each ureter is a 25–30 cm retroperitoneal muscular tube. Urine is pushed down mainly by peristalsis — waves of smooth-muscle contraction, 1–5 per minute, faster when urine forms faster — helped by the pressure from behind and by gravity. The ureters enter the back wall of the bladder obliquely, tunnelling through the muscle before opening; there is no valve, but as the bladder fills its internal pressure squashes these oblique tunnels shut, so urine cannot reflux up to the kidneys. When that mechanism fails, bladder bacteria can ascend and infect the kidney. The bladder is a hollow, highly distensible muscular bag behind the pubic bone; empty it collapses, full it rises pear-shaped into the lower abdomen and can hold 700–800 mL (less in women, where the uterus sits on top). Its wall is stretchable urothelium, a three-layered detrusor muscle, and an outer adventitia.

basics: This is the bladder cut in a coronal (front-to-back-facing) plane in a woman. The two ureters enter at the back corners of a smooth triangle on the bladder floor, the trigone, whose front corner is the exit into the urethra (internal urethral orifice). basics: The male urethra is ~20 cm, five times the female one, and is a shared duct for urine and semen. Seen in sagittal section it has three named parts on its way from the bladder neck to the tip of the penis. The prostatic urethra passes through the prostate gland just below the bladder and receives the ducts of the prostate and the ejaculatory ducts (sperm plus seminal-gland fluid). The intermediate (membranous) urethra is the shortest part, passing through the deep perineal muscles that form the voluntary external sphincter. The spongy (penile) urethra, the longest part, runs through the erectile corpus spongiosum of the penis to the external urethral orifice and receives the bulbourethral glands. The lining changes from urothelium near the bladder to columnar epithelium and finally stratified squamous at the tip. Clinically, an enlarged prostate obstructs flow here. basics: The embryo builds three successive pairs of kidneys from a strip of intermediate mesoderm along its back (the urogenital ridges), each more caudal and more advanced than the last. The pronephros (week 3–4) never functions and vanishes by week 6, but leaves its duct. The mesonephros takes over that duct (now the mesonephric duct) and works briefly before regressing by week 8. Around week 5 a side-branch of the mesonephric duct, the ureteric bud, grows into the metanephric mesoderm; the bud branches to form the ureter, pelvis, calyces and collecting ducts, while the mesoderm it invades forms the nephrons — so the collecting system and the nephrons have different origins and must connect. The cloaca, the common end-chamber of gut and urinary tracts, splits into a rectum behind and a urogenital sinus in front that becomes the bladder and urethra. The kidneys start in the pelvis and ascend to the lumbar region; failures give horseshoe, ectopic or absent kidneys.
